item.title: How to Use OpenCode on Windows for FREE (Install + First Project)
item.description:
Most OpenCode install guides for Windows still tell you to run npm install -g opencode-ai. Run that today and you get version 1.19. The current OpenCode is version 2, and it ships under a different npm package: @opencode/cli.

This guide installs the right version on Windows 11, connects a free AI model without paying anything, and builds a small working app from one prompt. You don’t need a GPU, because the model runs in the cloud.

This is part 1 of my OpenCode series. Everything later in the series builds on this setup.

🎥 Watch the Video

👉 Watch on YouTube: How to Use OpenCode on Windows for FREE

🧠 What Is OpenCode?

OpenCode is an open-source AI coding agent that runs in your terminal. You describe what you want in plain English. It reads your project, writes files and runs commands. It’s an open-source alternative to Claude Code, and you pick the model: a free one, a paid one with your own API key, or a local model through Ollama.

🧰 What You Need

  • Windows 10 or 11
  • Node.js (OpenCode installs with npm)
  • A terminal. I use Windows Terminal with PowerShell.

OpenCode runs natively on Windows, but the official docs recommend WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux) for the best experience. For a beginner, native Windows is the simplest way to start, so that’s what this guide uses.

1️⃣ Step 1: Check Node.js

Open PowerShell and run:

1
2

node -v
npm -v

If both print a version number, you’re ready. If not, download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, install it with the defaults, then close and reopen your terminal. An old terminal window won’t see the new install.

2️⃣ Step 2: Install OpenCode V2 (the Right Package)

This is where most tutorials go wrong. If you installed OpenCode before, remove the old V1 package first, then install V2:

1
2
3

npm uninstall -g opencode-ai     # only if you installed V1 before
npm install -g @opencode/cli
opencode --version               # should start with 2

If the version starts with 1, the old package is still on your machine. Uninstall it and run the install again.

Two more things:

  • The V2 docs say Windows package managers (Scoop, Chocolatey, winget) aren’t supported. Use npm.
  • If you prefer a normal app window, there’s a Windows desktop app on the OpenCode download page. This guide uses the terminal version.

3️⃣ Step 3: Open a Project

OpenCode works on whatever folder you start it in. Create a new one and launch it:

1
2
3

mkdir expense-tracker
cd expense-tracker
opencode

The prompt box at the bottom of the OpenCode screen is where you type.

4️⃣ Step 4: Connect a Free Model 

1
2

/connect   -> OpenCode -> sign in
/models    -> pick a free model

Type /connect, choose OpenCode and sign in with your OpenCode account. Then type /models and pick one of the free models. OpenCode’s docs list several models as free for a limited time, including Big Pickle and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Free.

Two honest notes:

  • The free list changes, so check /models for what’s free today.
  • Some free models may keep your prompts to improve the model. Don’t paste client code, passwords or API keys into a free model. For practice projects, it’s fine.

If you already have an API key from OpenAI, Anthropic or Google Gemini, /connect is also where you add it.

5️⃣ Step 5: Plan vs Build

OpenCode has two main agents, and beginners often miss this:

Agent What it does
Build (default) Writes code, edits files and runs commands
Plan Explores your project and writes a plan. It doesn’t edit your project files.

Press Shift + Tab to switch between them. My rule: start every new task in Plan, read the plan, then switch to Build. It costs one extra step and saves a lot of undoing.

🚀 Your First Project: An Expense Tracker From One Prompt

In Plan mode, paste this prompt:

1
2
3
4

Plan a simple expense tracker web app using HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
I want to add an expense with an amount in rupees, a category and a date,
see the monthly total, and save everything in the browser's localStorage.
Keep it in three files.

Read the plan. If it looks right, press Shift + Tab to switch to Build and type: Go ahead and build it.

When it finishes, open index.html in your browser. Add an expense and check that the total updates. Then refresh the page: if the data is still there, localStorage is working. The video shows the full run.

⌨️ Shortcuts Worth Learning on Day One

Shortcut What it does
@ + file name Attaches a file to your prompt, e.g. @style.css add a dark mode
/undo Reverts your last message and the changes that came with it
/redo Brings an undone change back
! + command Runs a terminal command without leaving OpenCode, e.g. !dir
Esc Stops the agent mid-task
Ctrl + P Opens the command menu

⚠️ Honest Limits

  • Free models change and have limits. If one stops working or slows down, open /models and pick another.
  • Native Windows vs WSL. Native works, but the official recommendation is WSL for better file performance and terminal support. If you hit odd terminal problems, WSL is the fix.
  • Build runs commands without asking by default. OpenCode’s permission rules allow everything unless you add rules. If you want it to ask before every shell command, add an ask rule for shell (see Permissions). Either way, use Git or a test folder until you trust it.

🛠️ Quick Fixes

Problem Fix
opencode is not recognized Reopen the terminal. Still failing? Run npm config get prefix and add that folder to your PATH.
“Running scripts is disabled on this system” Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned
Version shows 1.x npm uninstall -g opencode-ai, then npm install -g @opencode/cli
No free models in /models Run /connect, choose OpenCode and sign in first

❓ FAQ

Is OpenCode free? OpenCode itself is open source and free. The models are separate: OpenCode offers some free models for a limited time, and paid models need your own API key or credits.

Do I need a GPU? Not for this setup. The free models run in the cloud. You only need a GPU if you run a local model, which is the next video.

Why does opencode --version show 1.x? You installed the old opencode-ai package. Uninstall it and install @opencode/cli.

Should I use WSL instead? The official docs recommend WSL for the best experience. Native Windows is simpler for a first setup, and you can switch later.

⏭️ Next in the Series

Next up: OpenCode + Ollama. You’ll run a model on your own PC, so you don’t need an account or an internet connection for the model. Subscribe to The Code Street so you don’t miss it.

item.title: Can a 1.7B Model Be an AI Agent? Building a Local Agent with LFM3 + Ollama
item.description:
Imagine running an AI agent on your own computer, without paying for expensive APIs, without sending your data to the cloud, and without a 70-billion-parameter model.

Can a model with just 1.7 billion parameters actually behave like an agent? Can it calculate numbers, check the weather, manage files, save notes and complete several tasks on its own?

That’s the question I set out to test with LFM3, the small model from Liquid AI. I built a complete local agent around it using Ollama, Node.js and React, and then gave it real work. The full walkthrough is on YouTube, and this post covers the same ground in written form.

🎥 Watch the Video

👉 Watch on YouTube: Can a 1.7B Model Be an AI Agent?

The Four Parts

The app has four components:

  1. React frontend. This is where you talk to the agent and watch what it’s doing.
  2. Node.js backend. It talks to the model, handles requests and runs the execution loop.
  3. Ollama. It runs LFM3 locally on your machine.
  4. JavaScript tools. These are the functions the agent can call: a calculator, a weather lookup, file access and notes.

The key idea is the loop between them. The model decides what should happen, the backend executes the operation, and the result goes back to the model.

Tool Calling: The Model Chooses, Your Code Executes

A language model is good at understanding instructions and generating text. On its own, it can’t check live weather, read a file or run a calculation in your app. Tool calling fills that gap.

You give the model a list of tools. Each tool has a name, a description and a set of parameters. When the model needs a calculation, it replies with a structured request, for example:

1
2
3
4

{
  "name": "calculator",
  "arguments": { "expression": "7800 * 0.18" }
}

The model is not doing the math. It is asking the application to run the calculator. The backend checks the arguments, calls the real JavaScript function, and gets back 1404. That result goes to LFM3, which turns it into a normal reply.

The model never gets unrestricted access to your computer. It can only request the tools you have registered.

One Request, Several Tools

Calling one tool is useful. The more interesting case is a single instruction that needs several steps:

Check the weather in Mumbai, calculate 18% GST on 7,800 rupees, save a note about the result, and prepare a summary.

The model works through it in order:

  • Weather: requests the weather tool for current conditions.
  • Calculator: calculates 18% GST, which is 1,404 rupees, for a total of 9,204 rupees.
  • Save note: stores the result.
  • Summary: writes the final answer from the tool results.

The sequence is not hardcoded in the frontend. The model reads the tool descriptions and decides what to call. The backend keeps the loop going, running tools and returning their results, until the model has a final answer. That loop is what separates an agent from a chatbot.

Watching the Agent Think: Live Events and Metrics

I didn’t want a black box where you send a message and wait. The app streams progress to the frontend with Server-Sent Events (SSE). You can see when the request arrives, when LFM3 starts, which tool it selected, when the JavaScript runs, and what came back. If a tool fails, the error shows up in the same timeline.

The dashboard also records performance:

  • Tool execution time, measured around the actual JavaScript function.
  • Time to first token (TTFT), how quickly the model starts answering.
  • Tokens per second, from Ollama’s response metadata.

These numbers come from the running application, not from a demo.

Safety Is Not Optional

Giving an agent tools means controlling what those tools can do. The app uses several guardrails:

  1. Allow-list. The model can only call tools registered in the app.
  2. Argument validation. Arguments must match the tool’s schema before anything runs.
  3. No eval, no arbitrary shell. Maths goes through a dedicated expression parser.
  4. File sandbox. File operations stay inside one workspace folder.
  5. Human approval. Sensitive actions, like deleting a file, pause until a person approves or denies them.

The approval step matters most. An agent should have the minimum permissions it needs, and anything sensitive should stay under human control.

Adding Your Own Tool

Extending the agent means adding a JavaScript function. In the walkthrough I add a roll_dice tool: I register its name, a description, the number of sides as a parameter, and a short implementation that returns a random number from 1 to that count. After restarting the backend, the agent finds the tool in its list. Asking it to “roll a six-sided dice” makes LFM3 pick the tool, supply the argument, and return the JavaScript result.

The model gets a new capability without retraining or changing its architecture. You extend the agent with your own code.

The Real Test

The demo uses one prompt that needs several tools:

Check the weather in Bengaluru, calculate 18% GST on 7,800 rupees, save a note containing the calculation result and today’s date, and prepare a summary.

The agent calls the weather tool, runs the GST calculation, saves the note and then writes a summary. The weather lookup uses an external data source. The model inference runs locally through Ollama.

Performance and Limits

LFM3 is not trying to replace large coding or reasoning models. Here’s what it handles well and where it struggles:

Strengths Limits
Classification Complex reasoning
Structured extraction Tasks that need broad world knowledge
Simple automation Occasionally picks the wrong tool
Lightweight, focused agents Sometimes gives invalid arguments

Tool calling is not perfect every time. That’s why validation, error handling and approval matter. Tool execution and model inference also take very different amounts of time. A calculator finishes almost instantly, while generating a reply takes longer. Watch both.

Takeaways

Can a 1.7-billion-parameter model behave like an agent? Yes, within the right boundaries. It won’t outperform larger models. But you can connect a small local model to your own functions, limit what it can touch, and get real work done.

The pattern in one line:

The model asks for a tool. Your code executes it. The result goes back to the model.

If you want to build something like this, start with one tool, add validation, and only then add more. I’d love to hear what you would build with a local agent. Tell me in the comments on the video.

Thanks for reading, and see you in the next one.
